newsitem.title: USA: U.S. probes suspected transfer of secrets to Israel.
newsitem.headline: U.S. probes suspected transfer of secrets to Israel.

text.p: Federal agents seized computers, financial records and other documents from the home of a suburban Detroit tank engineer who is suspected of having divulged U.S. military secrets to Israel for the past 10 years, the FBI disclosed on Wednesday.

Special Agent Dawn Moritz said no criminal charges have been filed in the investigation of David Tenenbaum, 39, a mechanial engineer for the United States Army Tank, Automotive and Armaments Command in Warren, Michigan.

But in an affidavit filed in U.S. District Court in Detroit, FBI Special Agent Sean Nicol said there may be reason to believe that Tenenbaum violated federal laws on espionage, counter intelligence and computer crimes.
"The matter is still under investigation," Moritz said. "There have been no arrests to date."

TACOM's Tank Automotive Research and Development Engineering Centre, north of Detroit, provides design, engineering and support services for the Army's tracked and wheeled vehicle programmes, ranging from the top-of-the line M1-A2 Abrams tank to the "Humvee" off-road vehicle.
The installation, located on the grounds of the now-closed Detroit Arsenal Tank Plant, also performs some weapons development work for future combat vehicles.
The FBI said in the affidavit that Tenenbaum admitted to divulging non-releasable classified information to every Israeli liaison officer assigned to TACOM over the last 10 years.

The information Tenenbaum disclosed included Patriot missile countermeasures data, ceramic armour data, armour test and survivability data and unreleasable classified information on the Bradley Fighting Vehicle and the Humvee, according to the affidavit.

Tenenbaum made the admissions after a polygraph test that was part of a background check for a higher security clearance, according to the affidavit, which lists him as a mechanical engineer on TACOM's Combat Vehicle Team.
The FBI said Tenenbaum admitted that he "inadvertently" gave information to the Israeli officers and to Reuven Granot, Scientific Deputy Director of the Israeli Ministry of Defence.
He also admitted that he has taken documents labeled "For Official Use Only" and "Secret" to his home in Southfield, Michigan. Calls to his home on Wednesday were unsanswered.
"This matter is currently in the preliminary stages of an investigation. Importantly, no one has been arrested or charged with a crime," the U.S. Embassy in Israel said in a statement.
A spokesman for the Israeli Consulate in Chicago was not available for comment on the matter.
The Israeli Defence Ministry said its personnel were under orders not to accept any secret U.S. information.

"All Ministry of Defence and Israeli Defence Forces officials in the U.S.A. are under the most explicit and categorical instructions to decline any and all offers of classified U.S. information," the ministry statement said.

In the Feb. 15 search of Tenenbaum's home, according to court documents, FBI agents seized two personal computer systems, computer disks, financial and tax records, telephone records and several documents relating to armour systems.
